title: Magnetic Field — 60 MCQs
description: Topics: magnetic field lines & flux, Oersted, forces on charges and current-carrying conductors, torque on coils, moving-coil galvanometer, Hall effect & probes, Biot–Savart, Ampère's law, and force between conductors (definition of ampere).

questions.q: Magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying conductor (viewed in plane) are:
options: Concentric circles centered on the conductor
questions.explanation: Biot–Savart and Ampère's law show B encircles the conductor; lines are concentric circles around wire.

questions.q: Direction of magnetic field around a straight conductor is given by:
options: Right-hand rule: thumb in current direction, fingers show B
Left-hand rule with thumb opposite current
Use compass pointing away from wire
questions.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule gives circular B direction around conductor.

questions.q: Magnetic flux Φ through an area is defined as:
options: Scalar product of E and A
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux is surface integral of magnetic flux density (B) over area; SI unit Weber (Wb).

questions.q: Sketchable qualitative field lines inside a long ideal solenoid are:
options: Uniform nearly parallel lines inside and nearly zero outside
questions.explanation: Long solenoid produces nearly uniform axial B inside and weak external field—field lines are parallel inside.

questions.q: Oersted's experiment demonstrated that:
options: Electric current produces a magnetic effect (deflects compass needle)
questions.explanation: Oersted observed current in wire causes nearby compass needle deflection—current produces magnetic field.

questions.q: Limitation of Oersted's original experiment is that it:
options: Did not quantify field strength or direction fully and used qualitative compass deflection
questions.explanation: Oersted's work was qualitative demonstration; later laws (Biot–Savart) gave quantitative B expressions.

questions.q: Magnetic flux density B has SI unit:
questions.explanation: B (magnetic flux density) unit is Tesla; 1 T = 1 Wb/m².

questions.q: Magnetic flux through a closed surface is:
questions.explanation: Magnetic monopoles not observed; net flux through closed surface is zero (∇·B=0).

questions.q: Sketch of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet shows lines emerging from:
options: North pole and entering at south pole outside the magnet
questions.explanation: Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet and continue through inside from south to north.

questions.q: Magnetic flux linkage for a coil of N turns is defined as:
options: N times magnetic flux through one turn (NΦ)
questions.explanation: Flux linkage = NΦ; appears in Faraday's law for induced emf.

questions.q: Force on a charge q moving with velocity v in magnetic field B is given by:
options: F = q (E + v × B) only for electric field
questions.explanation: Lorentz magnetic part: magnetic force is q times cross product, perpendicular to v and B; magnitude qvB sinθ.

questions.q: Magnitude of magnetic force on moving charge is:
questions.explanation: Cross product magnitude yields q v B sin of angle between v and B.

questions.q: A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is:
questions.explanation: If v is parallel (θ=0), sinθ=0 so magnetic force is zero; motion unchanged by B.

questions.q: Force on a straight conductor of length L carrying current I in uniform B (angle θ between L and B) is:
options: F = I L B sin θ
F = I L B cos θ
questions.explanation: Conductor force is vector sum of forces on moving charges; magnitude I L B sinθ with L vector direction of current.

questions.q: Direction of force on current-carrying conductor in magnetic field is given by:
options: Right-hand thumb rule used for B direction only
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule gives direction of force: thumb-force, forefinger-field, middle-current.

questions.q: If a conductor is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field and current reverses direction, force on the conductor:
questions.explanation: Force ∝ I; reversing current reverses force direction (cross product sign flips).

questions.q: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform B-field undergoes:
questions.explanation: Magnetic force perpendicular to velocity provides centripetal force leading to circular motion radius r = mv/(qB).

questions.q: Radius of circular path of charge q, mass m, speed v in B is:
questions.explanation: Set q v B = m v²/r → r = m v/(q B).

questions.q: Cyclotron frequency (angular) for charge q in B is ω = qB/m. This frequency is independent of:
questions.explanation: ω = qB/m doesn't depend on velocity in non-relativistic regime; period independent of energy.

questions.q: Work done by magnetic force on a moving charge over displacement is:
questions.explanation: Magnetic force is perpendicular to instantaneous velocity, so does no work; kinetic energy unchanged.

questions.q: Torque on a rectangular coil (area A) with N turns carrying current I in uniform B (plane makes angle θ with B) is:
options: τ = N I A B sin θ
τ = N I A B cos θ
questions.explanation: Magnetic moment μ = N I A; torque τ = μ × B = N I A B sinθ.

questions.q: Maximum torque on rectangular coil occurs when coil plane is:
options: Parallel to magnetic field (so normal is perpendicular) giving sinθ=1
questions.explanation: Torque ∝ sinθ where θ is angle between coil normal and B; maximum at θ=90° meaning coil plane parallel to B.

questions.q: Moving-coil galvanometer measures small currents by detecting:
options: Torque on coil in magnetic field balanced by spring restoring torque causing angular deflection
questions.explanation: Current in coil produces magnetic torque; equilibrium with torsion spring gives deflection proportional to current.

questions.q: D'Arsonval (moving-coil) galvanometer is preferred because of:
options: High sensitivity, linear scale, and low restoring torque
questions.explanation: Moving-coil galvanometers are precise and have linear response and good sensitivity.

questions.q: To increase sensitivity of moving-coil galvanometer you can:
options: Increase number of turns, stronger magnetic field, increase coil area, reduce spring constant
questions.explanation: Magnetic torque ∝ N I A B; increasing N, A, B or reducing restoring constant increases deflection per current.

questions.q: Moving-coil galvanometer is converted to voltmeter by:
questions.explanation: Series resistor limits current for given voltage so galvanometer deflection corresponds to voltage.

questions.q: Moving-coil galvanometer converted to ammeter requires:
options: A suitably low-value shunt across the coil
questions.explanation: A shunt bypasses most of current so galvanometer measures a fraction, enabling higher current measurement.

questions.q: Sensitivity in terms of current for a galvanometer (S_I) is often given as:
questions.explanation: Current sensitivity is physical deflection per unit current; used for calibration.

questions.q: Dead time / damping in a galvanometer refers to:
options: Oscillatory vs overdamped response; damping reduces oscillations and speeds settling
questions.explanation: Damping (e.g., electromagnetic) determines transient behavior; critical damping gives fast settling without overshoot.

questions.q: Moving-coil galvanometer has linear response when deflection angles are small because:
options: Restoring torque is proportional to angular displacement (Hooke's law) and magnetic torque ∝ current
Magnetic field varies strongly with angle
questions.explanation: Small-angle linearity arises from torsion spring torque ∝ angle and magnetic torque ∝ I (assuming uniform B and coil geometry).

questions.q: Hall effect produces a transverse voltage across a current-carrying conductor when placed in a magnetic field; the Hall voltage is proportional to:
options: B I / (n e t) (for charge carrier density n, thickness t)
questions.explanation: Hall voltage V_H = (B I)/(n q t) where q is carrier charge (e for electrons), t thickness; shows linear dependence on B and I.

questions.q: In Hall effect derivation, equilibrium transverse electric field E_H balances magnetic force on carriers: q v_d B = q E_H. The Hall voltage VH across thickness t is:
options: V_H = E_H t = (B I)/(n q t)
questions.explanation: Using drift velocity v_d = I/(n q A) with A = width×t yields VH = (B I)/(n q t).

questions.q: Sign of Hall voltage indicates:
options: Sign of dominant charge carriers (positive for holes, negative for electrons)
questions.explanation: Polarity of Hall voltage reveals whether carriers are positive or negative.

questions.q: Hall probe measures magnetic flux density B by:
options: Measuring Hall voltage at known current and probe geometry and using VH = BI/(n q t) or calibrated sensitivity
questions.explanation: Practical Hall sensors are calibrated to give B from measured VH for given excitation current.

questions.q: A Hall probe is preferred for measuring B in localized regions because it:
options: Provides point measurement of B including direction (polarity) and works in DC fields
Measures average over large volume only
questions.explanation: Hall probes give local B measurement and polarity, useful for mapping field distribution.

questions.q: If thickness t of Hall element decreases (all else constant), Hall voltage for same B and I:
questions.explanation: VH inversely proportional to thickness t, so thinner element yields larger VH for given I and B.

questions.q: Hall coefficient R_H is defined by R_H = E_H/(J B) and equals:
questions.explanation: R_H = 1/(n q) for single-carrier type; used to determine carrier concentration.

questions.q: Hall effect can be used to determine carrier concentration n by measuring:
options: VH, current I, B, and thickness t (and using VH = BI/(n q t))
questions.explanation: Measuring VH for known I, B, t yields n since VH = BI/(n q t).

questions.q: In typical semiconductor Hall sensor, sensitivity depends on:
questions.explanation: Sensor sensitivity influenced by material properties (n, mobility) and geometry (thickness, contact placement).

questions.q: Hall probe calibration often yields a linear relation VH = k B for fixed I; the factor k depends on:
options: Probe geometry and excitation current and material properties
questions.explanation: Calibration factor k encapsulates 1/(n q t) times I and geometry; must be measured.

questions.q: Biot–Savart law gives magnetic field dB due to small current element I dl at point r as:
questions.explanation: Biot–Savart: contribution of current element to B with vector cross product, distance squared denominator.

questions.q: Magnetic field at centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying current I (single loop) is:
questions.explanation: On axis at center, single loop field magnitude is μ0 I /(2R) directed along axis.

questions.q: Magnetic field near long straight conductor at distance r is given by Ampère/Biot–Savart as:
questions.explanation: Field outside long straight current is μ0 I /(2π r) circling conductor (Ampère law).

questions.q: Magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid (n turns per unit length) carrying current I is:
options: B = μ0 n I (approximately uniform inside)
questions.explanation: Long solenoid field is μ0 n I inside (n = N/L), nearly uniform, nearly zero outside.

questions.q: Superposition principle applies to magnetic fields because:
options: Magnetic fields from different sources add vectorially
questions.explanation: B fields obey linear superposition (sum of contributions from currents).

questions.q: For a circular coil of N turns, field at centre is:
questions.explanation: N turns add field linearly: N times single loop's B.

questions.q: Application of Biot–Savart law is most convenient for:
options: Calculating field from finite current elements and loops where symmetry not sufficient for Ampère's law
questions.explanation: Biot–Savart is direct, applicable for finite geometries; Ampère easier for high symmetry (infinite wire, solenoid).

questions.q: Direction of magnetic field at point due to small current element dl is perpendicular to both dl and vector to point according to:
questions.explanation: Cross product yields direction perpendicular to plane formed by dl and r vector.

questions.q: Magnetic field at a point on axis of a finite circular coil (radius R) at distance x from plane (single loop) is:
questions.explanation: Standard result for on-axis field of current loop; reduces to μ0 I/(2R) at center x=0.

questions.q: For long solenoid of finite length, edge effects cause:
options: Field outside not exactly zero and internal field slightly non-uniform near ends
questions.explanation: Finite solenoids have fringing fields; ideal long solenoid assumption neglects end effects.

questions.q: Ampère's circuital law states that the line integral ∮ B · dl around a closed path equals:
questions.explanation: Integral of B around closed loop equals μ0 I_enc (in vacuum) — basis of Ampère's law.

questions.q: Using Ampère's law, magnetic field at distance r from an infinitely long straight wire is derived as:
questions.explanation: Choose circular Amperian loop concentric with wire; B constant on loop yields result.

questions.q: Magnetic field inside an ideal toroid (N turns, current I, mean radius r) at radius r is:
questions.explanation: Ampère's law around circular path inside toroid gives B (2π r) = μ0 N I => B = μ0 N I /(2π r).

questions.q: A toroidal solenoid has negligible external field because:
options: Ampère loops outside enclose net zero current (windings cancel)
questions.explanation: Currents around torus produce field confined inside; external path encloses equal forward/back currents giving net zero.

questions.q: Force per unit length between two long parallel conductors separated by distance d carrying currents I1 and I2 is:
questions.explanation: Derived from fields of one wire acting on other; used to define ampere.

questions.q: Parallel currents in same direction experience:
questions.explanation: Magnetic fields cause force that attracts parallel currents flowing same direction.

questions.q: The ampere is defined in SI (old definition) via force between two parallel conductors as: two infinite parallel conductors 1 m apart, carrying 1 A each, experience force per metre equal to:
questions.explanation: By definition, 1 A produces force 2×10⁻7 N per metre between two long parallel conductors 1 m apart in vacuum.

questions.q: Using Ampère's law, field inside infinite straight solenoid with n turns per unit length is derived assuming:
options: B is uniform inside and tangential field outside ~0 (high symmetry)
questions.explanation: Choose rectangular Amperian loop partly inside solenoid; interior contributes μ0 n I.

questions.q: Magnetic torque on rectangular coil is used in electromechanical meters because torque ∝:
options: N I A B (magnetic moment × B)
questions.explanation: Torque magnitude equals magnetic moment (NIA) times B, used to drive pointer in meters.

questions.q: Magnetic flux linkage change NΦ with time induces emf given by Faraday's law:
options: ε = − d(NΦ)/dt (magnitude depends on rate of change)
questions.explanation: Faraday's law: induced emf equals negative rate of change of flux linkage (Lenz's law gives minus sign).
